utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could the registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is IT-01-48-PT, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, counsel. For the Prosecution appear Mrs. Marie Tuma, trial attorney, Mr. Hasan Younis, trial support, and I, Ekkehard Withopf, acting senior trial attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Appearing for Mr. Sefer Halilovic, attorney Ahmet Hodzic. The other members of the Defence team are not present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This matter is listed as a Pre-Trial Conference in this case. The history is a long one, but the position which we need to work towards is this: That this case is the first or may well be the first reserved case in the list of cases, and it should therefore be ready, if at all possible, for hearing in the autumn. The complications, we know particularly on the Defence side, and we will consider them. We will also consider any matters as far as the Prosecution are concerned. And it may be simplest to begin with them. And Mr. Withopf, let us begin with your motion to add two witnesses. We'd be inclined to grant that, but we need to consider the application. In fact, we'll grant it, but it will have to be considered in the light of the overall number of witnesses who -- which you're entitled to call. The first matter that we have to consider or one of the matters that we have to consider under Rule 73 bis. Now, will you help us with this: No doubt you've been considering the -- you've been considering the number of witnesses who you -- you want to call. How many live witnesses now is it that you propose to call, Mr. Withopf?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution is proposing 57 live witnesses and 45 witnesses under Rule 92 bis. Live witnesses are 24 crime-base-related witnesses, 17 in relation to the first crime base, Grabovica, and 7 in relation to the second crime base, namely Uzdol. 33 of such witnesses concern notice and knowledge issues, and in particular, as Your Honours are certainly aware of, the issue of command and control, which is -- will be one of the most crucial issues in this case. Five witnesses have been added after the filing of the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief in mid-June last year. There's some likelihood that very few additional witnesses the Prosecution wishes to add. In relation to the necessity, Your Honours - and you already addressed it - of the high number of witnesses, there are a number of characteristics to this case which require such a high number of witnesses. We have very few eyewitnesses in relation to both crime sites, since almost nobody survived the two massacres. We have four for Grabovica and five for Uzdol. In each case, however, such witnesses have only witnessed portions of the crime. The Trial Chamber will get the full picture only after all eyewitnesses have been heard. In addition, the Prosecution, and that particularly relates to the Grabovica crime, has to rely on a number, on a significant number of witnesses which fall under the category of so-called insider witnesses. Ten of such witnesses are alone from the ABiH 1st Corps 9th Mountain Brigade, the brigade which allegedly is responsible for the killings. Again, in order to get the full picture and to get all bits and pieces of the evidence, it appears to be necessary that such witnesses have also to be heard. And finally - and that is one of the main concerns of the Prosecution - this will be the first case which is a pure Article 7(3) case, meaning command responsibility alone. We have to prove full notice and knowledge. We have to prove full notice and knowledge in relation to both crime sites. And in addition, we have to fully prove all elements which constitute the elements of Article 7(3) of the Statute in regard to both failure to prevent and failure to punish in respect to all -- to both crime sites. We calculated the length of the examination-in-chief, and the result is that we think within 41 days we will have covered -- we will have examined in chief all live witnesses for the Grabovica crime base incident we anticipate about three weeks; for the Uzdol crime base incident, about four days; and for notice of command and control issues, about five weeks. We have one military expert, as you certainly are aware of, and two pathologists, one for Grabovica and one for Uzdol. We anticipate one day in examination-in-chief for the military expert and also one day for both pathologists. That means we anticipate in some 43 days for examination-in-chief, which means almost -- well, about nine weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We can return to the -- well, witnesses in a moment. Help us with matters of disclosure. As we understand the position - as I understand it, I should say - there is some previous statements of witnesses which have not been disclosed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct. That concerns the so-called prior statements under Rule 66(A)(ii) obviously. Very few of such statements have been disclosed in the past; however, the Prosecution over the last few days made significant efforts, and these efforts have results to the extent that today we will disclose 87 of such prior statements of 38 witnesses; 63 prior statements of 24 live witnesses; and 24 prior statements of 14 Rule 92 bis witnesses. That means a significant portion of such prior statements will be disclosed today after this conference. The searches will obviously continue, the ISU searches. They will generate results. There's an internal deadline for the live witnesses end of July, meaning within two to three weeks. For the Rule 92 bis witnesses, there's an internal deadline end of August this year, meaning that by end of August, beginning of September we anticipate to be in a position to have disclosed all prior statements. One must also keep in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mind that quite a number of the Prosecution witnesses will not have any prior statements at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Withopf, are those prior statements in B/C/S language?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Most, if not all of such statements, are statements taken by the local authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they are as such, in B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So disclosure, then, we can be satisfied will be finished by the end of August for all the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: That concerns the Rule 66(A)(ii) disclosure. It will be somewhat different in respect to the Rule 68 disclosure exculpatory materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll come to that. The two -- the two experts have not been disclosed in B/C/S; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, there is some positive development. In respect to the expert report of our military expert, General Ridgway, the expert report has been made available to the Defence on 31st of March this year. It has been disclosed, again in English language, on 10th of July. And the B/C/S translation, in the language of the accused obviously, has also been disclosed on 10th of July, meaning last week. The military expert report of General Zorc, will be disclosed today, immediately after this conference in both, in English and in B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: However, you're going to call one only in the -- meaning General Ridgway.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Correct. The Prosecution intends to call only one military expert, namely General Ridgway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the pathologist's report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The pathologist report, Your Honours, were part in B/C/S language of the indictment supporting materials, meaning such reports have been disclosed one and a half years ago, and the full English translation has been made available to the Defence on 14th of March this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That brings us back to the witnesses. Now, Judge Kwon may have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Among 57, after having -- having a brief and quick look on those statements, I got the impression that some -- some of them appeared to appear more suitable for the admission under Rule 92 bis. So if I can give the witness numbers in 65 ter, those will be Witness number 2, 3, 5 -- I'm sorry, I'm mistaken. Witness number 2, 3, 5, 29, 30, 53, 54, those witnesses are for the Grabovica. And Witness number 1, 8, 15, and 27, apparently for Uzdol. And Witness number 9, 19, 20, 26, 36, 47, 48, and 49, those are for -- those witnesses are for general matters. I think they could be considered for admission under Rule 92 bis, and you can make your observation later. And if I can add one thing more: You named among the Rule 92 bis witnesses Witness number 44 and Witness number 37. They appear to me that they have direct knowledge of the acts and conduct of the accused, and thus I think they should give evidence as viva voce witnesses. If you can -- if you have any observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I certainly tend to agree in respect to the two 92 bis witnesses you just mentioned. In respect to the witnesses from the live witness list, Your Honours wish to move them from the live witness list to the Rule 92 bis witness list. The Prosecution would appreciate if we could make our submissions in written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So having said that, I have in mind that limiting the total number of live witnesses to a maximum of 40. So you can when you make your submissions also refer to that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution, in preparation of this Pre-Trial Conference, already considered limiting the number of witnesses. We considered at first instance between five to ten witnesses, what comes somewhat close to your proposal. And I also notified that a number of such witnesses are such ones you just proposed. However, we would like to make our written submissions in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Withopf, we'll obviously need to consider these matters. And it may be that we'll not be able to make an order today for the number of witnesses. It may be appropriate for us to adjourn consideration of that when we've dealt with the matters for the Defence. Is there anything more you want to add at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Not in respect to witnesses, but I understand you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. wish also to cover the situation on the Rule 68 disclosure of exculpatory materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. I'd overlooked that. What is the position there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Rule 68 exculpatory material, disclosure of such material is obviously an ongoing obligation. Several volumes of such materials have been disclosed in the past. Amongst such materials, the obvious ones the trial team knows about. Another Rule 68 disclosure has been done last Thursday, and today we will disclose further Rule 68 materials, about 75 additional Rule 68 documents will be disclosed. However, Rule 68 ISU searches, using about some 75 search criteria, have not yet been completed. More material obviously will follow. Recent inquiries with ISU have revealed that a completion of the Rule 68 searches using our search criteria can, in the best-seen scenario, only be expected within the next four months, probably four to five months. That's because of the fact that other cases which are in trial or cases which have already a scheduled trial date are higher in the priority. It, as always, comes down to a matter of resources. The Prosecution, however, would like to use this occasion to again invite the Defence to suggest search criteria for Rule 68 searches. Such criteria could actually limit and accelerate the ISU searches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would be necessary to expedite this process, if -- if there's a date in the autumn, because it clearly should be ready for trial. If you would convey to those who have charge of these matters that there is the -- the position of this case and its necessary priority and the fact that the Trial Chamber has expressed the view that it should be ready for trial in September, which would give you two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: We are very well aware of the situation, and we will do everything what can be done to accelerate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Hodzic, we know your position, that you've come into this case very late in the day. You've had, we recognise, difficulties in progressing the matter. We hope that your various applications to the Registry for co-counsel and for further assistance can be met in order that this case can be made ready for trial. The Prosecution have virtually finished now their disclosure to you, so that is not at the moment an outstanding problem or not a large one. But we recognise that there are problems for time on your side. Having heard about the position of the case, when do you think you might be -- you could make it ready for trial, given that you get the resources you've asked for and given that you have the assistance, which I understand you should be getting, of a co-counsel? With a view to having it -- may I say this: With a view to starting it in the autumn of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before this conference, I submitted a motion in writing in which I set out all the problems that I have encountered when I took over the defence of Mr. Sefer Halilovic. Unfortunately, I have to say that at this point I am not in a situation to continue with the defence of Mr. Sefer Halilovic because too little time is left for me to understand the case, analyse it, and provide Mr. Halilovic with a proper and fair defence. I have been working on this case for only four months. I have used most of those four months for writing submissions because there were a number of omissions in the previous proceedings. And this has had a negative effect on the gathering of materials for the defence of Mr. Sefer Halilovic. In no case can I be ready, not because I don't want to but because objectively I am not able to be ready for trial before six to eight months have elapsed. I beg the Chamber to bear in mind that I have not had the benefit of co-counsel, and when I discussed undertaking the defence of Mr. Sefer Halilovic I said very clearly that I would be able to take up his defence provided I had co-counsel to assist me in the proceedings because I did not know what the procedure was before this Tribunal. I have many years of experience, but in a completely different legal system. In view of the volume of material collected, both by the Defence and presented by the Prosecution, I have not yet managed even to read it all, let alone study it, analyse it, find what the important points are in order to provide a competent defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, may I interrupt you. If you were to be assigned co-counsel within the very near future, say within the next two or three weeks, what would your estimate be as to when you would be ready? You earlier said six to eight months. Would it be the same estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I said in my written submission, and I repeat it now. This is the time I estimate it would take me, provided I was given co-counsel. Without co-counsel, I cannot proceed at all. I regret to have to say this, Your Honours, but that's what the circumstances are. I can say that I have now been abandoned by my assistant, so that simply I have to deal with all this on my own. I am the only person on this team competent to prepare a defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll have to consider the position. Is there anything else you want to raise with us, Mr. Hodzic? Any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very important issue is the financial issue, which I expect will be resolved, because the team depends on this. Also, I would ask the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to receive these submissions in the Bosnian language sooner, so that we can prepare for particular witnesses and documents on time. Otherwise, I have no other issues to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I speak for myself. It's no reflection what I'm going to say on Mr. Hodzic. He's been brought into this case late. But the fact that cases are not ready for trial is a matter of real concern to the Tribunal. It's wrong that accused are not brought to trial promptly, and it's equally wrong if it is the Defence who are not ready. And it should be understood that the Defence have an obligation to be ready on time for trials. Nonetheless, in the particular circumstances of this case, having regard to the difficulties which Mr. Hodzic personally has faced, through no fault of his, we are prepared to accede to his motion that he has more time to this extent, that we say that this case is not to be listed for trial for another six months. This Pre-Trial Conference will be adjourned to a date to be fixed. The Prosecution have leave to call two additional witnesses, to complete disclosure of all matters within five months, and to make submissions within 28 days on the number of witnesses who they wish to call. Mr. Withopf, is that enough time for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's certainly enough time for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And we'll consider the matter in due course. Now, Mr. Hodzic, you can have another six months. But, of course, as you understand, you must be ready then. The matter of co-counsel is one which I understand can be resolved fairly rapidly. And, of course, it's subject to that and also subject to the matter of more funds being made available. But provided those matters are resolved, we shall expect you to be ready in six months' time. Yes. Unless there are any other matters -- senior legal officer, are there any other matters to be raised? No. Very well. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HODZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Pre-Trial Conference adjourned at
